c.tagline: Himalayan lake city of houseboats, shikaras, and Mughal gardens.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis run on fixed local union rates rather than meters, so confirm the fare before setting off; app-hailing (Uber) has only limited coverage. Shikara boats on Dal and Nigeen Lakes have government-set hourly rates.

emergency.note: 112 is India's single all-services emergency number; 108 is the ambulance line.

avoid.reason: Kashmir — periodic unrest and security operations; check advisories; avoid areas near the Line of Control

hood_desc: The lakefront tourist strip along Dal Lake, lined with houseboats, hotels, and shikara ghats; the classic first-timer base, with the Mughal gardens and Shankaracharya Hill all close by.
Srinagar's central commercial hub and clock-tower square, packed with shops, bakeries, and mid-range hotels; convenient and lively but congested, and the historic heart of the city's civic life.
A leafy, upscale riverside residential district along the Jhelum, with quieter guesthouses, cafes, and easy access to the centre; good for a calmer stay away from the tourist crowds.

A tranquil garden suburb on the eastern shore of Dal Lake beside the famous Nishat and Shalimar Mughal gardens, with lake-view resorts and mountain backdrops; suits travelers wanting calm and scenery.

The dense historic core (Nowhatta, Khanyar, Zaina Kadal) around Jamia Masjid and centuries-old Sufi shrines, papier-mache workshops, and covered bazaars; the most atmospheric but least touristed area.

water.note: Stick to bottled or filtered water, including on houseboats.

sys.n: Srinagar city buses (JKSRTC / Smart City electric buses)

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver; auto-rickshaws are usually negotiated rather than metered, and shikara rides on Dal Lake have government-set hourly rates. There is no rechargeable transit card system.
transit.hours: City buses and autos run roughly 7am-8pm; after dark taxis are the main option and shikaras stop running.
transit.note: Public transport is limited; most visitors get around by prepaid taxi, auto-rickshaw, or shikara on the lake. Traffic in the Old City and around Lal Chowk is heavily congested.

train: Srinagar Railway Station on the Banihal-Baramulla (Kashmir Valley) line, connecting to the national network via the Jammu-Baramulla railway
bus: TRC / Batmaloo bus stand - JKSRTC and private intercity buses to Jammu, Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg and (seasonally) Leh
ferry: Shikara and passenger boats on Dal and Nigeen Lakes (local only)

airport.name: Srinagar International Airport (SXR)
rentals: Local operators only (no major international brands)

transit.m: Prepaid taxi to the city centre / Dal Lake (30-45 min)
No rail or metro link; some hotels offer shuttles

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up or leaving ~5-10% for good service is appreciated but not required.

landmarks: Dal Lake
Srinagar's shimmering centrepiece, where cedar houseboats, floating gardens and paddled shikaras drift beneath Himalayan peaks in scenes unchanged for centuries.
Shalimar Bagh
Emperor Jahangir's 1619 'abode of love', the grandest Mughal garden in Kashmir, terraced with fountains, chinar trees and pavilions above Dal Lake.
Nishat Bagh (Garden of Bliss)
Twelve cascading terraces of roses, fountains and giant chinars tumble toward Dal Lake, framed dramatically by the Zabarwan mountains behind.
Shankaracharya Temple
An ancient hilltop Shiva temple crowning Takht-e-Suleiman hill, rewarding the climb with the definitive panorama of Srinagar, Dal Lake and the Himalayas.
Hazratbal Shrine
Kashmir's holiest Muslim shrine, a gleaming white-marble mosque on Dal Lake's shore believed to preserve a hair of the Prophet Muhammad.
Jamia Masjid
A monumental 14th-century mosque in the old city, its prayer hall supported by 378 towering deodar pillars beneath distinctive pagoda-like spires.
Pari Mahal (Palace of Fairies)
A romantic seven-terraced Mughal garden and ruined observatory perched on Zabarwan slopes, glowing at dusk high above Dal Lake.
Chashme Shahi
The smallest and most refined of Srinagar's Mughal gardens, built in 1632 around a mountain spring famed for its sweet, restorative water.
Khanqah-e-Moula (Shah-e-Hamdan Shrine)
A gorgeously painted wooden shrine on the Jhelum River, founded in 1395 and covered in papier-mâché reliefs and intricate Kashmiri woodwork.
Hari Parbat Fort
An 18th-century Afghan-era fortress crowning a sacred hill ringed by Hindu, Muslim and Sikh shrines, overlooking the entire old city.

train.note: No international trains - the Line of Control is closed. The Kashmir valley line runs from Baramulla through Srinagar to Banihal, and since the Chenab bridge and the USBRL link were completed the valley is now connected to the national network, with through services toward Katra and Jammu. Book on IRCTC; check current status, as the line closes in heavy snow and during security disruptions.

bus.note: There is no international coach - the cross-LoC Srinagar-Muzaffarabad bus has been suspended since 2019. Domestic buses and shared Sumo jeeps run from the Srinagar TRC and Batmaloo stands to Jammu (10-12 hours on the national highway), Leh in the summer season and Gulmarg or Pahalgam for day trips. The Srinagar-Leh road is normally open only from about June to October.

ferry.note: There are no scheduled ferries. Shikara boats on Dal and Nigeen lakes are the local water transport, used to reach houseboats and the floating gardens, and are hired by the hour rather than run to a timetable.

half.name: Gulmarg
half.blurb: Hill station with a high-altitude cable car and meadows that turn into a ski resort in winter.

half.name: Yusmarg
half.blurb: Quiet alpine meadow ringed by pine forest, less visited than Kashmir's larger hill stations.

full.name: Pahalgam
full.blurb: Valley town used as a base for pony treks and hikes into the surrounding pine-covered mountains.

full.name: Sonamarg
full.blurb: High-altitude meadow valley near glaciers along the road that continues toward Ladakh.
